# Sūciloma Sutta (Snp 2.5 (PTS Snp 47))

**ID:** Snp 2.5 (PTS Snp 47)  
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Sūciloma Sutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sūciloma Sutta* is the fifth discourse of the Cūḷavagga ("Small Chapter") in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 2.5, PTS p. 47) [Anderson and Smith 1913; Norman 1997-2001]. Set at the stone couch (*taṅkitamañca*) in Gayā, the text comprises an introductory prose narrative followed by four verses (vv. 270–273) [Anderson and Smith 1913; Dhammika, Middle Land, Middle Way; Levitt 2009]. The yakkha Sūciloma ("Spiky" or "Needle-haired"), in the company of another yakkha named Khara, seeks to test whether the Buddha is a genuine ascetic [DeCaroli 2004; Saddhatissa 2013]. Sūciloma presses his body against the Buddha, who draws back, remarking that the yakkha's touch is disagreeable [DeCaroli 1999; Levitt 2009; Saddhatissa 2013]. Sūciloma threatens to disrupt the Buddha's mind, split his heart, or throw him across the River Ganges if he fails to answer his questions [Bailey, The Raven And The Serpent; Norman 1997-2001]. In response to Sūciloma's inquiry regarding the origins of passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dosa*), delight, aversion, and errant thoughts, the Buddha explains that these defilements arise from within oneself (*ito*, glossed by the commentary as *attabhāvato*), like shoots growing from the trunk of a banyan tree [Hamilton 1996; Norman 1997-2001].

The sutta possesses an exact canonical duplicate in the *Yakkha Saṁyutta* (SN 10.3) [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003]. Verses from the sutta are also cited in several sections of the *Niddesa* (Mnd 1, 14, 16; Cnd 23). In Sanskrit, verse equivalents are preserved in the canonical *Śarīrārthagāthā* embedded in the *Yogācārabhūmi* [Martin 2006].
